source.title_on_document: Why unequal AI access enhances team productivity: the mediating role of interaction processes and cognitive diversity

supplement.holds: The main article identifies writing-task instructions in Supplementary Section 1 (p. 6, Section 3.3), evaluator instructions and high- and low-scoring sample submissions in Section 2 (pp. 6-7, Section 3.4.2.1), and interaction-process coding categories in Section 3 (p. 7, Section 3.4.4). The saved PDF contains no supplement. No additional statistics or standard-error tables can be confirmed; requests to the named supplement link and the article DOI failed with WinError 10013. These descriptions come from the main article, not an inspection of the external supplement.

paper_design_summary: In a laboratory experiment, 120 Chinese university students formed 60 two-person teams and first wrote a press release without AI. Teams were then randomly assigned to unequal Kimi access (one member) or full access (both members) for a second press release; the no-AI phase always preceded the AI phase and used a different product prompt (pp. 5-7, Sections 3-3.3 and Figure 3). Marketing professionals graded the writing, and an embedding measure compared the two teammates’ spoken contributions (pp. 6-7, Sections 3.4.2.1 and 3.4.3).

studies.label: Laboratory team press-release experiment: unequal versus full AI access, with a common no-AI baseline

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were randomly formed into two-person teams. Teams were randomly assigned to unequal versus full AI access for the treatment-phase task; within unequal-access teams, the member permitted to use AI was also randomly selected. The no-AI task was a common first phase, not a third randomized arm, and condition order was not randomized (pp. 5-6, Sections 3 and 3.2; p. 7, Figure 3).
assignment.quote: Then, in the treatment phase, these teams were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: only one member could use GenAI (unequal access), or both members could use it (full access).
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 3 Method, opening paragraph; Section 3.2; p. 7, Figure 3.

Arm-specific randomized and analyzed people counts are not printed and are left null; team counts have not been converted into people counts.

The analyzed count refers to that reported common sample, not a separate post-exclusion baseline count. This is not an independent randomized arm and must not be added to the AI-phase sample (p. 6, Sections 3-3.3; p. 7, Figure 3; p. 11, Table 3 shows baseline team groups).

The paper reports an experimental sample of 120 people, formed into 60 two-person teams, and demographic analyses with N = 120 (pp. 5-6, Sections 3-3.1). Table 3 reports the baseline team groups as N = 40 and N = 20 (p. 11), and the writing evaluation includes 120 submissions (p. 7, Section 3.4.2.1). The submissions and nine expert raters are not additional experimental participants; the phases do not create separate samples.
participants.who: Undergraduate and graduate students from various majors at a university in China, collaborating face to face in two-person teams (pp. 5-6, Sections 3 and 3.1).

ai_tool.name_model: Kimi 3.0, developed by Moonshot, as named by the document (p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Authorized team members received a link to Kimi with no restriction on how to interact with it. Everyone had task instructions and basic document-editing tools; other websites and applications were prohibited unless instructed. On-site recordings were reviewed for compliance (p. 6, Section 3.2).

task.description: Teams collaboratively wrote a 700-character Chinese press release about an electric bicycle in the no-AI phase and AR glasses in the AI phase. Basic product information and writing instructions were supplied. The different prompts and fixed order are acknowledged limitations (p. 6, Sections 3.2-3.3; p. 14, Section 5.4).
task.duration: Each writing task was limited to 45 minutes (p. 6, Section 3.3).

outcomes.name: Task quality: overall expert grade, with originality-only robustness measure
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Blinded marketing professionals assigned an overall grade from 1 to 7 based on writing quality, content quality, and originality. Nine professionals evaluated the 120 submissions, with three raters per submission and 40 submissions per rater; Cronbach alpha = 0.791 (pp. 6-7, Section 3.4.2.1). Coded as usefulness because the main measure is an overall task-quality grade, not an explicitly named overall-creativity rating. In Section 4.4.2, originality is used as the sole indicator of task quality in a robustness mediation model; it is retained here as a novelty-focused variant of the same outcome under form rule 7 (pp. 10-11; p. 12, Figure 6). Writing quality and content quality have no separately reported outcome results. The main OLS analysis reports N = 120 submission observations (p. 9, Table 1); this is not a count of independent teams. The originality mediation model instead reports N = 60 (p. 11). The observation is one team-task submission, so unit is output, while assignment is by team. The paper names task quality as a dependent variable but does not explicitly designate primary or secondary outcomes; primary is therefore not_stated (p. 8, Section 4).

contrasts.reported: Task quality: unequal access M = 5.654, SD = 0.080; full access M = 5.250, SD = 0.118; t = 2.881, p < 0.01 (p. 8, Section 4.1). Table 1, Model (1), prints Full access to AI b = −0.4023**, adjacent column headed SD = −2.2771; N = 120, adj. R² = 0.170. Its footnote calls the adjacent numbers t statistics and ** means p < 0.05; no usable SE for this total comparison is explicitly supplied (p. 9). Indirect effect via cognitive diversity: b = −0.283, SE = 0.091, 95% CI [−0.513, −0.134]; serial indirect effect via negative socio-emotional reactions and cognitive diversity: b = −0.061, SE = 0.029, 95% CI [−0.148, −0.021] (p. 9, Sections 4.2-4.3.1; p. 10, Table 2). Originality-only robustness: serial indirect effect b = −0.105, SE = 0.050, 95% CI [−0.248, −0.036]; cognitive diversity-to-originality path b = 4.619, SE = 1.346, p < 0.01 (p. 11, Section 4.4.2). No arm means or total/direct AI contrast for originality are printed. Regression signs are copied unchanged: unequal access is the reference group, so negative full-access coefficients favor unequal access. SE/CI availability here refers to mediation results, not the main total contrast. Table 3 condition counts of 40 and 20 are baseline teams, not arm-level people counts or newly established AI-phase observation counts (p. 11; p. 10, Section 4.4.1).
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.1; p. 9, Figure 4A, Table 1 Model (1), and Sections 4.2-4.3.1; p. 10, Table 2; pp. 10-11, Section 4.4.2; p. 12, Figure 6; p. 6, Section 3.4.1 (reference coding); p. 11, Table 3 (arm N values are teams).

contrasts.reported: Unequal access M = 5.654, SD = 0.080; no access M = 4.981, SD = 0.094; t = −5.103, p < 0.01 (p. 8, Section 4.1). Table 1, Model (1), prints No access to AI b = −0.6730***, adjacent column headed SD = −5.1990; N = 120, adj. R² = 0.170. Its footnote describes t statistics and *** means p < 0.01 (p. 9). Numeric signs are as printed, with unequal access as regression reference. This compares the later unequal-access task with the common earlier no-AI phase; no-AI observations also include teams later given full access. It is not a randomized AI-versus-no-AI comparison or an after-AI outcome. Figure 4 labels its bars as one standard error of the mean, whereas the prose calls these dispersions SDs; the labels are preserved without resolving that inconsistency (p. 9, Figure 4 caption).
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.1; p. 9, Figure 4A and Table 1 Model (1); p. 6, Sections 3-3.3 and 3.4.1; p. 7, Figure 3.

outcomes.name: Cognitive diversity between the two teammates’ spoken contributions
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Audio-recorded team discussions were transcribed and manually corrected. Each member’s utterances across the whole discussion were concatenated, encoded with the Universal Sentence Encoder, and normalized to unit length. Cosine distance between the two members’ vectors measures cognitive diversity (p. 7, Section 3.4.3). The scored outputs are spoken contributions by different people within a team, not final press releases across teams. The reported PROCESS model N = 60 is used for n_units (p. 8, Section 4), with teams as the analytical units; the paper does not reconcile this with the repeated no-AI and AI phases. Models that replace task quality by originality or change the interaction-concentration measure remain robustness analyses of this same diversity measure (pp. 11-12, Sections 4.4.2-4.4.3 and Figures 6-7). Cognitive diversity is a mediator in the paper, but no explicit primary/secondary outcome designation is given; primary is therefore not_stated (p. 8, Section 4).

contrasts.reported: Unequal access M = 0.631, SD = 0.011; full access M = 0.510, SD = 0.018; t = 5.938, p < 0.01. Mediation-model direct path for full access relative to the unequal-access reference: b = −0.107, SE = 0.025, p < 0.01 (p. 9, Section 4.2). SD labels are copied from the prose; the Figure 4 caption describes its error bars as ±1 standard error of the mean. Larger cosine distance means greater diversity, and the negative coefficient is full minus unequal access, not a negative effect of unequal access. The mediation model prints N = 60 (p. 8, Section 4); Table 3 reports 40 and 20 baseline teams (p. 11). Neither establishes independent person-level precision for these estimates.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 4.2 and Figure 4C; p. 10, Figure 5; p. 7, Section 3.4.3; p. 8, Section 4 (model N); p. 11, Table 3 (arm N values are teams).

contrasts.reported: Unequal access M = 0.631, SD = 0.011; no access M = 0.609, SD = 0.012; t = −1.299, p = 0.197. Mediation-model direct path for no access relative to the unequal-access reference: b = −0.017, SE = 0.020, p > 0.1 (p. 9, Section 4.2). The no-AI observations come from the earlier common baseline, including teams later assigned full access; this is not randomized AI-versus-no-AI evidence. The paper reports independent-sample t-tests despite the repeated-phase design (pp. 8-9, Section 4.2). The mediation model prints N = 60 (p. 8, Section 4), but the article does not explain its rows across both phases.
contrasts.locator: pp. 8-9, Section 4.2; p. 9, Figure 4C; p. 10, Figure 5; p. 6, Sections 3-3.3; p. 7, Figure 3.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance d(W_i, W_j) = 1 − cos(W_i, W_j) between normalized vectors; larger values indicate greater cognitive dissimilarity (p. 7, Section 3.4.3).
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Universal Sentence Encoder (USE), TensorFlow Hub; no model version or specific module URL is given (p. 7, Section 3.4.3).
diversity_detail.computed_over: The two members of each team: each person’s utterances are concatenated across the entire discussion, and the two resulting vectors are compared. This is within-team, between-person semantic distance; it is not all pairs of submitted press releases within an experimental arm (p. 7, Section 3.4.3).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Independent-sample t-tests across conditions (pp. 8-9, Section 4.2) and PROCESS/path-analysis coefficients with SEs (pp. 8-10, Section 4 and Figure 5). Figure 4 error bars are labeled ±1 SEM, whereas the prose calls the accompanying dispersions SDs. The PDF does not explain how repeated observations of the same team are handled for the no-AI comparisons; no participant- or team-clustered SE procedure is stated.
diversity_detail.notes: Retained as across_people because the computed measure compares contributions from different people, but its scope is the two collaborating teammates, not homogenization across independent teams’ final products. No similarity-to-diversity sign reversal was performed: the measure is already a distance. Negative regression coefficients use unequal access as the reference (p. 6, Section 3.4.1).

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria through the randomized comparison of unequal versus full Kimi access (ai_design): teams were randomly assigned to one-member or two-member GenAI access for their own press-release writing (p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2). The reported experimental sample is 120 people in 60 two-person teams (pp. 5-6, Sections 3-3.1); 120 submissions were rated and the main task-quality analysis reports N = 120 output observations (p. 7, Section 3.4.2.1; p. 9, Table 1). Table 3 represents both baseline team groups (p. 11; p. 10, Section 4.4.1). The analyzed people count retains the stated experimental sample; no separate post-exclusion people total is supplied, and repeated outputs and expert raters are not added to it. Blinded experts score the submitted press releases on task quality including originality, with originality also used alone in a robustness analysis (pp. 6-7, Section 3.4.2.1; pp. 10-11, Section 4.4.2). The common no-AI task always preceded AI use and used a different prompt, so its comparisons do not meet the random-assignment criterion (p. 6, Sections 3.2-3.3; p. 14, Section 5.4). The remaining questions about precision, supplementary measurement details, and cross-paper sample overlap do not change these three eligibility decisions.

one_line_finding: Unequal AI access produced higher expert-rated press-release quality than full access (5.654 versus 5.250; t = 2.881, p < 0.01; p. 8, Section 4.1) and greater semantic distance between teammates’ spoken contributions (0.631 versus 0.510; t = 5.938, p < 0.01; p. 9, Section 4.2).
open_questions: Are the dispersions labeled SD in Sections 4.1-4.2 standard deviations or standard errors? Figure 4 labels its bars as one standard error of the mean. Retain the printed labels; an unambiguous participant- or team-level SD is needed before standardization (pp. 8-9).
Table 1 labels its adjacent columns SD, includes negative entries, and says t statistics in the footnote. The intended precision labels and usable OLS standard errors need clarification (p. 9).

What are the analytical rows in the PROCESS models, which print N = 60, compared with the OLS N = 120? The same teams completed both phases, and independent-sample t-tests are reported. The handling of repeated team observations and independent-unit precision is not explained (pp. 6-11).
The external supplement could not be inspected. Its exact evaluation rubric, construction of the originality score, and any additional numerical results remain unconfirmed (pp. 6-7 and 14).

Does DOI 10.1002/pra2.1437 report the same participants? The candidate record flags a related conference version, but neither its full text nor an explicit sample-linkage statement was available. The saved PDF does not settle overlap.

open_items.item: Open question 1: Are the dispersions called SD in Sections 4.1-4.2 standard deviations or standard errors, given the SEM label in Figure 4 (pp. 8-9)? Authors would need to confirm the labels and provide an unambiguous team-level SD for standardization. This affects effect-size extraction, not any eligibility criterion; retain the printed labels pending clarification.

Open question 2: What precision statistic is intended by the SD columns in Table 1, which contain negative entries while the footnote says t statistics (p. 9)? Authors would need to identify the columns and supply usable OLS standard errors with their independent-unit basis. This affects precision and pooling, not any eligibility criterion.

Open question 3: What do the PROCESS N = 60 rows represent relative to OLS N = 120, and how are repeated team observations handled (pp. 6-11)? Authors would need to provide the model datasets or analysis code and explain phase inclusion and variance estimation. This affects interpretation and precision of the estimates, not any eligibility criterion: the reported 120-person experiment and the scored press-release dataset support eligibility independently of the unexplained mediation rows.

Open question 4: The external supplement remains uninspected; the exact evaluation rubric, originality-score construction, and any additional numerical results are unconfirmed (pp. 6-7, Sections 3.3-3.4.4; p. 14, Supplementary material). Inspection of the linked supplement, especially its evaluator instructions in Section 2, is needed. This does not affect the output-scoring criterion or either other criterion because the main article explicitly describes expert grading of participants' press releases and computed diversity of their spoken contributions.

Open question 5 and unresolved reconciliation.differences[6]: Does DOI 10.1002/pra2.1437 use the same participants? The candidate-record lead is unverified, the related paper could not be retrieved, and the saved journal article supplies no sample-linkage statement. Author confirmation identifying the shared or distinct participant samples would settle this. It affects cross-paper deduplication, not any of this paper's three eligibility criteria; neither overlap nor independence is established.
